introduction_markdown:
**GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD - General Certificate of Education Examination. JUNE 2025, ADVANCED LEVEL. English Language, Paper 2 (0730).**

Answer your questions either exclusively from **PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS)** or from **PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS)**.

**PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS) - Duration: Two and a Quarter Hours.** Instructions to candidates: ANSWER ONE QUESTION FROM EACH SECTION (Section A: Composition, Section B: Prescribed Texts, Section C: Creative Writing). ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you no marks.

**PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS) - Duration: Three Hours.** Instructions to candidates: Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will earn you little or no marks. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you little or no marks.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS) - SECTION B: COMPOSITION (20 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (06 marks); Expression (08 marks); Accuracy (06 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly, and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.enonce_markdown: **e)** Describe an incident that caused you to take the toughest decision you ever made and how it completely changed your life.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Opening: the Monday morning and the claim that the decision changed my life.
2. Background: the father's death and the family's poverty.
3. The easy money of the motorbike and its price.
4. The crisis: the teacher's question and the two choices.
5. The decision and how I felt.
6. How it changed my life.

**Model composition (541 words)**

The toughest decision of my life was made on a rainy Monday morning, on a motorbike that was not even mine. I was sixteen, and that decision completely changed my life.

My father, a carpenter, died suddenly of a stroke when I was in Form Four. He left my mother, my three younger sisters and a pile of debts. At the funeral, relatives promised to help, but within a month they had all disappeared. The rent was due, the workshop was closed, and my mother sold vegetables at the roadside for a few hundred francs a day. School fees were out of the question.

So I did what many boys in our neighbourhood do. A friend of my father lent me his old motorbike, and I began to carry passengers around town. The money was surprisingly good. Within two weeks, I was earning more in a day than my mother earned in three, and I could buy rice, pay the rent and even give my sisters pocket money. I felt proud, like a man who had saved his family. My friends from school called me a hero, and slowly I stopped thinking about the classroom.

Yet something troubled me. Each morning, as I passed the gate of my school, I saw my former classmates walking in with their books, and I felt a sharp pain in my chest. I had always wanted to become an engineer. At night, I lay awake calculating how long it would take to save the money for a better life, and the answer was always the same: never. The motorbike gave me today, but it would steal my tomorrow. Moreover, the work was dangerous; I had already fallen twice and seen a friend lose a leg.

The crisis came on that rainy Monday. As I waited for passengers, my old mathematics teacher, Mr Fon, stopped his car beside me. He did not scold me. He simply asked, "Is this where you want to be in ten years?" Then he told me about a scholarship fund for orphans in the parish, and he promised to buy my books himself. I could not answer. I rode in silence all day, and that night I told my mother everything.

The decision was terrible. If I returned to school, my family would lose my income and might go hungry. If I stayed on the motorbike, I would lose my future. My mother held my hands and said, "I did not give birth to a taxi driver. Go back to school. God will provide." Tears came to my eyes. The next morning, I returned the motorbike to its owner and put on my old uniform.

The following years were not easy. I studied at night by candlelight, washed cars at weekends, and my mother and sisters shared every small piece of bread. But the scholarship covered my fees, and I passed the GCE Ordinary Level with distinction, then the Advanced Level.

Today, I am a student of engineering, and I can help my sisters stay in school. That one decision turned a boy on the road to nowhere into a young man with a future. I learnt that the hardest choices, when made for the right reasons, open the widest doors.

**Marking grid (the paper prints the split of the 20 marks)**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 6 | A relevant treatment of the topic as set, a clear introduction, paragraphs that each develop one idea, a logical order and a conclusion |
| Expression | 8 | Varied sentence structures, precise vocabulary, suitable register and tone, good use of linking words, a convincing style |
| Accuracy | 6 | Correct grammar, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Writing fewer than 500 or more than 550 words, or ignoring the topic's exact wording (for example listing points instead of telling a story, or giving only one side when asked 'Do you agree?').
2. A weak plan: a long introduction, paragraphs that repeat one idea, no conclusion; or a pre-prepared composition that does not fit the question (it earns no marks).
3. Describing the decision without the reasons that made it so difficult, or saying 'it changed my life' without showing how.
